headline: Kings Point reads 73 degrees and the bass have gone nocturnal at the bridges
subhead: Warm, slack-tide Sound water has pushed the bass into a night bite while fluke and porgies carry the daylight hours.
body_markdown:
Guy at the bait shack on City Island asked me Tuesday why nobody's soaking bunker chunks off the bridge at noon anymore. Told him the same thing I've told every man who's asked me that question in thirty years on this water: because the fish aren't there at noon. Kings Point buoy's reading 72.9 this week, and when the western Sound gets that warm on top, the bass do what they've always done — they slide down onto structure and sulk through the daylight, then come up to hunt once the sun drops and the water cools a half a degree. This isn't news to anybody who's fished Execution Rocks longer than a season, but every August somebody forgets it, and every August I remind them.

So here's where the intel from the dock lines up with what I've seen with my own eyes off Hart Island and the Rocks the last ten days. The night bite at Throgs Neck Bridge has been the most reliable thing going. Eels — plain old live eels, snelled to a 1/0 or 2/0 circle hook, no weight or just enough to get them down into that current — fished tight to the pilings on the last two hours of the ebb. That's when the bait gets squeezed through the pilings and the bass are sitting right on the seam waiting for it. I had two nights this week where the first hour after dark was dead and then it turned on hard for about ninety minutes right around the bottom third of the tide. Fish in the 28 to 34 inch range, mixed slot and just-over, nothing monstrous but steady enough that three or four rods working the bridge on a weeknight put fish in the boat.

Execution Rocks is still doing its thing on the outgoing, same as it's done every summer I can remember, but you've got to work it at the right hour now. Forget the mid-afternoon troll — that's a bait-soaking exercise in August heat. Dusk into full dark, drifting bunker chunks or a whole live bunker on a fish-finder rig along the north side of the rockpile where the current rips hardest, that's your window. The bunker schools I flagged off Matinecock back in June haven't gone anywhere — if anything they've thickened up, and the blues have been all over them in open water off the point, blitzing on top some mornings before the sun's fully up. If you want bluefish, that's still the play — bunker spoons or wire leader with a bucktail teaser, fish where the birds are working, and don't wait around, because those pods move.

Now the good news, and it's genuinely good — fluke and porgy fishing is about as strong as it gets all year right now, and it doesn't care one bit about the bass going nocturnal. Stepping Stones and the reef structure off Matinecock Point have been holding porgies stacked up in 20 to 35 feet, and they're eating clam and squid strips on standard high-low rigs without much finesse required. Kids' trip, grandfather's trip, doesn't matter — that bite's been consistent right through the warm stretch. Fluke have been coming off the channel edges around Hempstead Harbor and the deeper drop-offs near Execution Rocks, working white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the last of the incoming when the current's still got some push to it but isn't ripping. Nothing giant — most fish 16 to 20 inches, a few keepers mixed in over 20 — but a satisfying pick if you're willing to drift a few different depths to find where they're stacked that day.

We flagged this last week — said the softer tides heading into the first quarter moon on August 5th would push the bass toward the strongest current hours and the deepest structure, and that's exactly what's playing out at the bridges right now. As that moon comes to first quarter this week, the tidal range is going to keep shrinking, which means less water movement, which means the bite windows get shorter and more concentrated. I'd rather fish a big tide any day, but a softer tide isn't a death sentence — it just means you've got to be precise about timing. Don't show up to Throgs Neck two hours before the tide change expecting fireworks. Show up right as the ebb hits its strongest push and fish through the last two hours of it. That's been the difference between a two-fish night and a skunk this week.

Weakfish have been a mixed bag — a few citations coming out of the deeper holes around Little Neck Bay on bucktails tipped with squid strips fished slow along bottom, but it's not a consistent pattern yet, more a bonus fish than something to plan a trip around. Blackfish season's still closed in most of these waters through the summer, so that's a fall conversation, though I'll tell you the rockpiles off Hart Island are going to be loaded once that opens back up.

Looking ahead, I don't see much reason for this pattern to break unless we get a real weather shift. High pressure's been stable, water's staying warm, and that means the night-bite-for-bass, day-bite-for-fluke-and-porgy split is going to hold through most of August. If I had one night this week to fish, I'd be at Execution Rocks on the outgoing starting an hour before sunset, working live bunker deep along the rock edge, and I'd have eels rigged as backup once it goes fully dark. Daytime, I'd be drifting bucktails off Matinecock for fluke while the porgies keep the rods bent between drifts. It's not a blitz-every-cast kind of week, but it's honest fishing, and if you respect the tide clock, you'll come home with something worth cleaning.
